options.text: Set `max_messages=1` in `BatchSettings`, so that the client sends each reading at once.
Publish each reading with its own ordering key, so that Pub/Sub sends the readings in parallel.
Increase `max_messages`, `max_bytes`, and `max_latency` in `BatchSettings`, within the request limits.
Call `future.result()` after each publish, so that the client sends one request at a time.

explanation: Batching **trades latency for throughput** and cost. The client sends a batch when it reaches any one threshold, and the Python default latency is only 10 ms. Higher thresholds put more readings in each request, and the consumers **accept up to one second** of delay.

whyWrong.A: This turns off batching, so each reading needs its own request.
whyWrong.B: Ordering keys add order, not batching. Ordered publishing also decreases publish availability.
whyWrong.D: This blocks the publisher after each message, which decreases throughput.

sources.title: Best practices to publish to a Pub/Sub topic
sources.evidence: The batching (or grouping) of messages helps the publisher to improve its efficiency and send messages at a higher throughput. Batching reduces the cost to publish data.

sources.title: Batch messaging
sources.evidence: To turn off batching in your client library, set the value of `max_messages` to 1.

stem: A subscriber runs in an on-premises data center. It can make outbound HTTPS connections, but it has no public HTTPS endpoint. It must process a large volume of messages from a Pub/Sub topic with high throughput. Which approach should you use?

options.text: A push subscription that sends the messages to the private IP address of the on-premises server.
A BigQuery subscription, and a job that reads the new rows from the table every few seconds.
A pull subscription, and a loop that calls the unary Pull API with the low-level client library.
A pull subscription, and a subscriber that uses the high-level client library with StreamingPull.

explanation: Pull fits a **large volume** and a subscriber with **no public HTTPS endpoint**, because the subscriber opens the connection. For most use cases, Google recommends the high-level client library with the StreamingPull API and asynchronous processing.

whyWrong.A: A push endpoint must be a public HTTPS server. Pub/Sub cannot push messages to private addresses.
whyWrong.B: This adds a table and a polling job. It also adds latency compared with direct delivery.
whyWrong.C: The low-level library has no lease management or flow control, so you must write them yourself. Google recommends StreamingPull for throughput.

sources.title: Choose a subscription type
sources.evidence: Large volume of messages (GBs per second). Efficiency and throughput of message processing is critical. Environments where it's not feasible to set up a public HTTPS endpoint with a non-self-signed SSL certificate.

sources.title: Pull subscriptions
sources.evidence: For most use cases, we recommend the Google-provided high-level client library with the StreamingPull API and asynchronous message processing.

sources.title: Create push subscriptions
sources.evidence: Pub/Sub operates outside of VPC networks and cannot directly push messages to private VPC addresses.

stem: A pull subscriber writes each message to a database. Sometimes the database is unavailable for several minutes. During these outages, the subscriber nacks each message, and Pub/Sub delivers it again at once. This fills the logs and wastes resources. No message may be lost. What should you do?

options.text: Acknowledge each message during an outage, and write it to a local file on the instance for a later retry.
Keep the nack, and set an exponential backoff retry policy on the subscription.
Keep the nack, and set the retry policy of the subscription to Retry immediately.
Stop the nack, and let each message wait for its 10-second acknowledgment deadline.

explanation: A nack makes Pub/Sub deliver a message again **immediately**, unless a retry policy sets a delay. With an exponential backoff retry policy, Pub/Sub waits longer between redeliveries, up to 600 seconds. The nack keeps the message in Pub/Sub, so **no message is lost**.

whyWrong.A: Pub/Sub discards an acknowledged message. If the instance stops, you lose the local file and the message.
whyWrong.C: Retry immediately is the default policy, which causes the current flood of redeliveries.
whyWrong.D: The client library continues to extend the deadline of a message that is not acknowledged. The messages hold the capacity of the subscriber, and no controlled delay occurs.

sources.title: Overview of the Pub/Sub service
sources.evidence: Nacking a message by a subscriber causes Pub/Sub to redeliver it immediately based on default retry settings, which can be modified.

sources.title: Subscription properties
sources.evidence: You can also set the value to Retry after exponential backoff delay. In this case, you must specify the maximum and minimum backoff values.

sources.title: Subscription properties
sources.evidence: The longest backoff duration that you can specify is 600 seconds.
